stops.date_confidence: Attested [A]: 200 delegates at Brand's Hall on 27 June 1905, with Debs, Mother Jones and Lucy Parsons among the speakers (Wikipedia, 'Big Bill Haywood'); libcom confirms the 'slaves of slaves' passage and that Parsons addressed the convention on two occasions. Two research entries claimed she was the only woman among the founders or the only woman to address the convention; both are false, since Mother Jones is named in the same sources, and are corrected here to one of two women. She also edited The Liberator in 1905 [A, Texas State Historical Association]. Coordinate corrected to the near North Side, Clark at Erie; the lens's 41.8977,-87.6533 lay roughly 1.8 km west.

stops.stop: Avondale, the Syndicalist League in her front room
stops.date_confidence: Attested [A] by Wikipedia: Parsons hosted the meeting establishing the Syndicalist League of North America in 1912, with William Z. Foster staying at her home at the time. The coordinate is corrected to her Avondale house: a research entry gave a generic Loop point that contradicted its own claim text and was reused for three unrelated stops. Month and day unknown, defaulted to 01-01. The League's size and equipment are [R].

stops.segment: The Wobbly and the Long Old Age
stops.stop: Halsted Street, the hunger march past Hull House
stops.date_confidence: Attested [A] by Wikipedia and the IWW archive biography: arrested in January 1915 with Father Irwin St John Tucker and nineteen others after speaking at a hunger march of roughly 1,500 unemployed on Halsted Street near Hull House. The day within January is not given in the sources and is chosen only to order the segment. The count of her arrests to that date is [R] and is stated as a minimum.

stops.segment: The Wobbly and the Long Old Age
stops.stop: Avondale, joining the Communist Party at eighty-eight
stops.date_confidence: Attested [A] by Wikipedia: blind, living in poverty in Avondale with a personal library of roughly 3,000 books, Parsons formally joined the Communist Party USA in 1939. Month and day unknown, defaulted to 01-01. Her reasons are not on record; the reading offered here is [R], inferred from her decade of prior work with Communist-led defence campaigns, which is itself [A].

stops.segment: The Fire and the Confiscated Library
stops.stop: Chicago, the last May Day
stops.date_confidence: Attested [A] by Wikipedia and the IWW archive biography: her last public appearance, as guest of honour at a May Day event with the Farm Equipment Workers' Organizing Committee, on 1 May 1941. No venue is named in any source reachable this session, so the canonical Chicago pin is used. That nothing she said was recorded is an argument from silence and is stated as such.

stops.segment: The Fire and the Confiscated Library
stops.stop: Avondale, the fire and the carts of books
stops.date_confidence: Death by house fire on 7 March 1942 at an age given variously as 89 or 91, and George Markstall's death of his injuries the following day, are attested [A]. The cause of the fire is disputed: Ashbaugh gives a wood stove, another account a basement water heater. The library's fate is deliberately split: police seizure of the books and papers from the gutted house is [A] per libcom, while FBI custody is [R] and contested, reaching us secondhand through Ben Reitman being told so by the head of the Chicago Red Squad, and the FBI itself denied any knowledge of the books. Part of the library burned rather than being taken. The coordinate is the Avondale house; one research lens had wrongly placed the death at the Loop pin.

stops.segment: The Fire and the Confiscated Library
stops.stop: Forest Home Cemetery, beside the monument she paid for
stops.date_confidence: Attested [A]: a memorial service attended by roughly 300 people and burial at German Waldheim (now Forest Home) Cemetery, Forest Park, near the Haymarket Martyrs' Monument, on 12 March 1942; the later interment of the ashes of Albert Jr. and George Markstall in her grave is [A] per the Forest Home Cemetery Overview. The Haymarket Martyrs' Monument by Albert Weinert was dedicated on 25 June 1893 [A]. The two research lenses gave conflicting coordinates for the cemetery (41.8703,-87.8241 and 41.86972,-87.81972); the first is used throughout this file and the discrepancy is left flagged rather than resolved.
